exampleAnswers.title: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
First, we let \[ I = \int \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{4x}\, \textrm{d}x. \]

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align} u = \ln^2 x &\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{4x} &\quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \int \dfrac{1}{4x} \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\ln x}{4} \,. \end{align}

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

\begin{align*} I &= \int \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{4x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \ln^2 x\left(\dfrac{\ln x}{4}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\ln x}{4} \right)\left(\dfrac{2\ln x}{x} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\ln^3 x}{4} -2\int \dfrac{\ln^2 x}{4x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\ln^3 x}{4} - 2I. \end{align*}

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end: \[\begin{align*} I &= \dfrac{\ln^3x}{4} - 2I \\[5pt] 3I &= \dfrac{\ln^3 x}{4} \\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{\ln^3 x}{12} + C \end{align*}\]

example.title: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
First, we let \[ I = \int \dfrac{\ln^8{x}}{x}\, \textrm{d}x. \]

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align} u = \ln^8{x} & \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{8\ln^7{x}}{x}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{x} & \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{1}{x} \textrm{d}x = \ln{x}\,. \end{align}

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

\begin{align*} I &= \int \dfrac{\ln^8{x}}{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \ln^8{x}\left(\ln{x}\right) - \int \left(\ln{x}\right) \left(\dfrac{8\ln^7{x}}{x} \right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \ln^9{x} - 8\int \dfrac{\ln^8{x}}{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \ln^9{x} - 8I. \end{align*}

Finally, we solve for $I,$ remembering to add a constant of integration $C$ at the very end: \[\begin{align*} I & = \ln^9{x} - 8I \\[3pt] 9I & = \ln^9{x} \\[3pt] I &= \dfrac{\ln^9{x}}{9} + C \end{align*}\]

example.title: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{1}^{e^{3}} \dfrac{\ln^4 x}{6x} \,\textrm{d}x$ using integration by parts. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{6x}\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align} u = \ln^4{x} & \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4\ln^3{x}}{x},\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{6x} & \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{1}{6x} \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\ln{x}}{6}. \end{align}

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

\begin{align*} I &= \int \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{6x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= (\ln^4{x})\left(\dfrac{\ln{x}}{6}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\ln{x}}{6}\right) \left(\dfrac{4\ln^3{x}}{x}\right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{6} - 4\int \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{6x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{6} - 4I. \end{align*}

Now, we solve for $I \mathbin.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral. \[\begin{align*} I & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{6} - 4I \\[5pt] 5I & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{6} \\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{30} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align*} \int_1^{e^{3}} \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{6x}\, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{30} \left(\ln^{5}{x} \right) \, \Bigg|_1^{e^{3}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{30}\left(\ln^{5}(e^{3}) - \ln^{5}(1)\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{30}\left((3\ln{e})^5 - 0^5 \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{30}\left(3^{5}-0\right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{81}{10}} \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_{1}^{e^{5}} \dfrac{\ln^4 x}{3x} \,\textrm{d}x$ using integration by parts. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{3x}\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align} u = \ln^4{x} & \quad \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4\ln^3{x}}{x},\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{3x} & \quad \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{1}{3x} \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\ln{x}}{3}. \end{align}

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

\begin{align*} I &= \int \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{3x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= (\ln^4{x})\left(\dfrac{\ln{x}}{3}\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\ln{x}}{3}\right) \left(\dfrac{4\ln^3{x}}{x}\right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{3} - 4\int \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{3x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{3} - 4I. \end{align*}

Now, we solve for $I \mathbin.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral. \[\begin{align*} I & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{3} - 4I \\[5pt] 5I & = \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{3} \\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{\ln^{5}{x}}{15} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align*} \int_1^{e^{5}} \dfrac{\ln^4{x}}{3x}\, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{15} \left(\ln^{5}{x} \right) \, \Bigg|_1^{e^{5}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{15}\left(\ln^{5}(e^{5}) - \ln^{5}(1)\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{15}\left((5\ln{e})^5 - 0^5 \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{15}\left(5^{5}-0\right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{625}{3}} \end{align*}

example.title: Integrating a Logarithmic Expression Using Cyclic Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I=\displaystyle \int \dfrac{\ln^3 z}{z}\, \textrm{d}z.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that

\begin{align*} u=\ln^3 z\quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}z} = \dfrac{3\ln^2 z}{z}\,,\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z} = \dfrac{1}{z}\quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \dfrac{1}{z} \,\textrm{d}z = \ln z. \end{align*}

Using the integration by parts formula, we get

\[\begin{align*} I &= \int \dfrac{\ln^3 z}{z}\, \textrm{d}z \\[5pt] &= \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}z}\,\textrm{d}z \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}z}\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &= \ln^3 z\left(\ln z\right) - \int \left(\ln z \right)\left(\dfrac{3\ln^2 z}{z} \right)\,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &=\ln^4 z -3\int \dfrac{\ln^3 z}{z}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \ln^4 z - 3I. \end{align*}\]

Now, we solve for $I \mathbin.$ We can ignore the constant of integration in this case, because it is insignificant for further evaluation of the definite integral. \begin{align*} I &= \ln^4 z - 3I \\[3pt] 4I &=\ln^4 z \\[3pt] I &= \dfrac{\ln^4 z}{4} \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align*} \int_1^e \dfrac{\ln^3 z}{z}\, \textrm{d}z &=\dfrac{1}{4} \left(\ln^4 z\right)\Biggr|_1^e\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\ln^4 (e)-\ln^4 (1)\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{x}\sin{x} - \int (\sin{x}) \left(e^{x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{x}\sin{x} - \int e^{x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= e^{x}\sin{x} - J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{x}\sin{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = e^{x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{x}\left(-\cos{x}\right) - \int \left(-\cos{x} \right)\left(e^{x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{x}\cos{x} + \int e^{x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{x}\cos{x} + I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= e^{x}\sin{x} - J\\[5pt] I &= e^{x}\sin{x} - \left( -e^{x}\cos{x} + I \right)\\[5pt] I &= e^{x}\sin{x} + e^{x}\cos{x} - I\\[5pt] 2I &= e^{x}\sin{x} + e^{x}\cos{x}\\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{e^{x}\sin{x} + e^{x}\cos{x}}{2} + C\\[5pt] \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-3x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -3e^{-3x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-3x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-3x}(\sin{x}) - \int (\sin{x}) \left(-3e^{-3x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = e^{-3x}\sin{x} + 3\int e^{-3x}\sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = e^{-3x}\sin{x} + 3J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-3x}\sin{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-3x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -3e^{-3x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-3x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-3x}\left(-\cos{x}\right) - \int \left(-\cos{x}\right)\left(-3e^{-3x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-3x}\cos{x} - 3\int e^{-3x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-3x}\cos{x} - 3I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= e^{-3x}\sin{x} + 3J\\[5pt] I &= e^{-3x}\sin{x} + 3\left( -e^{-3x}\cos{x} - 3I \right)\\[5pt] I &= e^{-3x}\sin{x}- 3e^{-3x}\cos{x} - 9I \\[5pt] 10I &= e^{-3x}\sin{x}- 3e^{-3x}\cos{x}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac{e^{-3x}}{10}\left(\sin{x} - 3\cos{x} \right) + C \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-2x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -2e^{-2x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-2x}\sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-2x}(-\cos{x}) - \int (-\cos{x}) \left(-2e^{-2x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2\int e^{-2x}\cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-2x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-2x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -2e^{-2x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-2x}\cos{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-2x}\left(\sin{x}\right) - \int \left(\sin{x} \right)\left(-2e^{-2x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2\int e^{-2x}\sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2J\\[5pt] I &= -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2\left( e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2I \right)\\[5pt] I &= -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2e^{-2x}\sin{x} - 4I \\[5pt] 5I &= -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2e^{-2x}\sin{x}\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-2x}}{5}\left(2\sin{x} + \cos{x} \right) + C \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin(3x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-x}\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(-\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3} \right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} \int e^{-x}\cos(3x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-x}\cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u = e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-x}\cos(3x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(\dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3}\int e^{-x}\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3}I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}J\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3}I\right)\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{9} - \dfrac{1}{9}I\\[5pt] %\dfrac{10}{9}I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] \dfrac{10}{9}I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x) + 3e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\left(\sin(3x) + 3\cos(3x)\right)}{10} + C \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Indefinite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{2x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} =2e^{2x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin(3x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{2x}\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{2x}\left(-\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3} \right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3} \right)\left(2e^{2x}\right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} \int e^{2x}\cos(3x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{2x}\cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{2x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2e^{2x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{2x}\cos(3x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{2x}\left(\dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \right)\left(2e^{2x}\right)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\sin(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}\int e^{2x}\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{2x}\sin(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}I. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting this back into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I.$ We remember to add a constant of integration $C$ at the end.

\begin{align*} I &= -\dfrac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}J\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{e^{2x}\sin(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}I\right)\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{2e^{2x}\sin(3x)}{9} - \dfrac{4}{9}I\\[5pt] %\dfrac{13}{9}I & = -\dfrac{e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{2e^{2x}\sin(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] \dfrac{13}{9}I & = \dfrac{2e^{2x}\sin(3x) - 3e^{2x}\cos(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac {e^{2x}\left(2\sin(3x) - 3\cos(3x)\right)}{13} + C \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Definite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle \int e^{-x}\sin(3x) \, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \sin(3x) \, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-x}\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(-\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3} \right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{3} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} \int e^{-x}\cos(3x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-x}\cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u = e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-x}\cos(3x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(\dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3}\int e^{-x}\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3}I. \end{align*}

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} I &= -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}J\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3}I\right)\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{9} - \dfrac{1}{9}I\\[5pt] %\dfrac{10}{9}I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] \dfrac{10}{9}I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x) + 3e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\left(\sin(3x) + 3\cos(3x)\right)}{10} \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align} \int_0^{\pi/3} e^{-x}\sin(3x) \,\textrm{d}x & = \left( -\dfrac{e^{-x}\left(\sin(3x) + 3\cos(3x)\right)}{10} \right)\Biggr|_0^{\pi/3}\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{e^{-\pi/3}\left(\sin\left(3 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + 3\cos\left(3 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)}{10} + \dfrac{e^{-0}\left(\sin\left(3 \cdot 0\right) + 3\cos\left(3 \cdot 0\right)\right)}{10}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3e^{-\pi/3}}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{3}{10}(e^{-\pi/3} + 1) \end{align}

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I = \displaystyle \int e^{-x}\cos(2x) \, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(2x) \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos(2x) \, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-x}\cos(2x)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(\dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2} \right) - \int \left(\dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(2x)}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \int e^{-x}\sin(2x) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(2x)}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-x}\sin(2x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u = e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(2x) \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin(2x)\, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{\cos(2x)}{2}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-x}\sin(2x) \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(-\dfrac{\cos(2x)}{2} \right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{\cos(2x)}{2} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(2x)}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\int e^{-x}\cos(2x)\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(2x)}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}I. \end{align*}

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} I &= \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(2x)}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}J\\[5pt] I & =\dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(2x)}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(2x)}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}I\right)\\[5pt] I & =\dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(2x)}{2} - \dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(2x)}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4}I\\[5pt] %\dfrac{10}{9}I & = -\dfrac{e^{-x}\cos(3x)}{3} - \dfrac{e^{-x}\sin(3x)}{9}\\[5pt] \dfrac{5}{4}I & = \dfrac{2e^{-x}\sin(2x) - e^{-x}\cos(2x)}{4}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac{1}{5}e^{-x}\left(2\sin(2x) - \cos(2x)\right) \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align} \int_0^{\pi/2} e^{-x}\cos(2x) \,\textrm{d}x & = \left( \dfrac{1}{5}e^{-x}\left(2\sin(2x) - \cos(2x)\right) \right)\Biggr|_0^{\pi/2}\\[5pt] & = \left(\dfrac{1}{5}e^{-\pi/2}\left(2\sin\left(2\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \cos\left(2\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \right) - \left( \dfrac{1}{5}e^{-0}\left(2\sin(2(0)) - \cos(2(0))\right)\right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{-\pi/2}}{5} + \dfrac{1}{5}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{-\pi/2} + 1}{5} \end{align}

example.title: Finding the Definite Integral of an Exponential-Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I= \displaystyle \int e^{-2x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-2x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -2e^{-2x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-2x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-2x}(\sin{x}) - \int (\sin{x}) \left(-2e^{-2x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2\int e^{-2x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-2x}\sin{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-2x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -2e^{-2x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-2x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-2x}\left(-\cos{x}\right) - \int \left(-\cos{x} \right)\left(-2e^{-2x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2\int e^{-2x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2I. \end{align*}

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} I &= e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2J\\[5pt] I &= e^{-2x}\sin{x} + 2\left( -e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 2I \right)\\[5pt] I &= e^{-2x}\sin{x} - 2e^{-2x}\cos{x} - 4I \\[5pt] 5I &= e^{-2x}\sin{x} - 2e^{-2x}\cos{x}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac{e^{-2x}}{5}\left(\sin{x} - 2\cos{x} \right) \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align} \int_{0}^{\pi/2} e^{-2x}\cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x &= \left( \dfrac{e^{-2x}}{5}\left(\sin{x} - 2\cos{x} \right) \right)\Biggr|_{0}^{\pi/2}\\[5pt] & =\left( \dfrac{e^{-2\pi/2}}{5}\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right) \right) \right) - \left( \dfrac{e^{-2(0)}}{5}\left(\sin{0} - 2\cos{0} \right) \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{-\pi}}{5} + \dfrac{2}{5}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{5}(e^{-\pi} + 2) \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I= \displaystyle \int e^{-x}\cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x). \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I &= \int e^{-x}\cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= (e^{-x})\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x)\right) - \int \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x)\right)(-e^{-x})\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\sin(3x) + \dfrac{1}{3}\int e^{-x}\sin(3x)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\sin(3x) + \dfrac{1}{3}J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-x}\sin(3x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

Let \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin(3x) \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x). \end{align*}

Then \begin{align*} J &= (e^{-x})\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x)\right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x)\right)(-e^{-x})\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\cos(3x) - \dfrac{1}{3}\int e^{-x}\cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\cos(3x) - \dfrac{1}{3}I. \end{align*}

Substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we solve: \begin{align*} I &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\sin(3x) + \dfrac{1}{3}J\\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\sin(3x) + \dfrac{1}{3}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\cos(3x) - \dfrac{1}{3}I\right)\\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{1}{3}e^{-x}\sin(3x) - \dfrac{1}{9}e^{-x}\cos(3x) - \dfrac{1}{9}I\\[5pt] 10I &= e^{-x}\left(3\sin(3x) - \cos(3x)\right)\\[5pt] I &= \dfrac{e^{-x}}{10}\left(3\sin(3x) - \cos(3x)\right). \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate the definite integral: \begin{align} \int_{0}^{\pi} e^{-x}\cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x &= \left(\dfrac{e^{-x}}{10}\left(3\sin(3x) - \cos(3x)\right)\right)\Biggr|_{0}^{\pi}\\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{e^{-\pi}}{10}(0-(-1))\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{10}(0-1)\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-\pi}}{10} + \dfrac{1}{10}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{10}\left(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-\pi} + 1}\right). \end{align}

question.explanation:
Let's denote the indefinite integral by $I= \displaystyle \int e^{-x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x.$

To use integration by parts, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \cos{x} \quad & \Rightarrow\quad v = \int \cos{x} \, \textrm{d}x = \sin{x}. \end{align*}

Then, using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} I & = \int e^{-x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}(\sin{x}) - \int (\sin{x}) \left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = e^{-x}\sin{x} + \int e^{-x}\sin{x} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = e^{-x}\sin{x} + J. \end{align*}

Again, we can use integration by parts to evaluate \[ J = \int e^{-x}\sin{x}\,\textrm{d}x. \]

To do this, let's suppose that \begin{align*} u=e^{-x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -e^{-x}\,, \\[5pt] \displaystyle\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = \sin{x} \quad & \Rightarrow \quad v = \int \sin{x}\, \textrm{d}x = -\cos{x}. \end{align*}

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get \begin{align*} J & = \int e^{-x}\sin{x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int u \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= uv - \int v \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= e^{-x}\left(-\cos{x}\right) - \int \left(-\cos{x} \right)\left(-e^{-x}\right) \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=- e^{-x}\cos{x} - \int e^{-x}\cos{x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -e^{-x}\cos{x} - I. \end{align*}

So, substituting this into our equation for $I,$ we can subsequently solve for $I\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} I &= e^{-x}\sin{x} + J\\[5pt] I &= e^{-x}\sin{x} + \left( -e^{-x}\cos{x} - I\right)\\[5pt] I &= e^{-x}\sin{x} - e^{-x}\cos{x} - I \\[5pt] 2I &= e^{-x}\sin{x} - e^{-x}\cos{x}\\[5pt] I & = \dfrac{e^{-x}}{2}\left(\sin{x} - \cos{x} \right) \end{align*}

Finally, we evaluate our definite integral, as follows: \begin{align} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{-x}\cos{x}\,\textrm{d}x &= \left( \dfrac{e^{-x}}{2}\left(\sin{x} - \cos{x} \right) \right)\Biggr|_{-\pi}^{\pi}\\[5pt] & = \left( \dfrac{e^{-\pi}}{2}\left(\sin{\pi} - \cos{\pi} \right) \right) - \left( \dfrac{e^{\pi}}{2}\left(\sin\left(-\pi\right) - \cos\left(-\pi\right) \right) \right)\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{-\pi}}{2} - \dfrac{e^{\pi}}{2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{e^{-\pi}-e^\pi}{2} \end{align}
